### Bettine Boltres

# Purchasing - The Person Who Makes the System Work


**You’re the person everyone calls when things get real. When a timeline tightens, when a supplier misses a shipment, when a deviation appears, when costs creep up, when someone says, “We need a decision by Friday” - it lands on your desk. And even when everything is running smoothly, you still don’t get to relax, because smooth today doesn’t guarantee stable six months from now.**


​


Your browser does not support HTML5 video.


This blog is for you, the purchasing professional who has to balance cost, quality, compliance, continuity, and credibility… all at the same time.


#### Your goals and objectives (what you’re actually trying to accomplish)


You’re not “just buying parts.” You’re protecting a supply chain, a budget, a program timeline, and ultimately a patient experience.


Your objectives are clear:


- Cost efficiency: You need the syringe system procured at the best possible value - without compromising quality or introducing risk.
- Quality assurance: You must select products and suppliers that meet strict quality standards and regulatory requirements.
- Supply chain resilience: You’re working to reduce supply disruptions and prevent delays that hit manufacturing schedules.
- Strategic partnerships: You want reliable supplier relationships that reduce firefighting and enable proactive planning.
- Regulatory compliance: Every procurement decision needs to align with regulatory standards and avoid compliance gaps.
- Negotiation leverage & inventory management: You’re looking to optimize contract terms and keep inventory under control - enough to ensure continuity, not so much that you’re tying up cash or creating waste.


That’s a lot of responsibility because each of those goals competes with the others unless the system is built to support you.


#### Your daily challenges (the hidden complexity behind “just source it”)


On paper, purchasing looks straightforward: define requirements, qualify suppliers, negotiate terms, secure supply. In reality, you’re navigating moving targets:


- Budget constraints: You’re under constant pressure to keep costs down while meeting high-quality demands.
- Operational complexity: Multiple components, multiple suppliers, multiple contracts, each with its own lead times, quality documentation, and change control realities.
- Vendor reliability: A supplier can look solid until they aren’t anymore, you risk quality drifts, late deliveries, inconsistent performance.
- Supply disruptions: Even small disruptions cascade and can put production planning, batch release timing, internal confidence, and external commitments at risk.
- Compliance issues: You have to ensure the suppliers maintain the right standards, documentation, and audit readiness, consistently.
- Communication complexity: Every additional supplier adds another interface: more coordination, more handoffs, more room for misalignment.


And what makes this harder is that you’re often managing these issues before they become visible. When you do your job well, nobody notices - until something breaks.


#### Your fears (what’s really at stake)


Let’s name the things that sit in the background of every sourcing decision—because you’re not imagining them.


- Product recalls: The nightmare scenario - quality problems leading to recall or market action, with downstream impact on patients and reputation.
- Budget overruns: When shortages, change requests, expedited shipments, and rework push costs beyond what you committed to.
- Compliance failures: A gap in documentation or quality system performance that becomes a regulatory issue at the worst possible time.
- Vendor disputes: Conflicts between suppliers - especially when responsibilities are fragmented - where accountability becomes a negotiation instead of a fact.
- Patient safety impact: The most serious fear: procurement decisions indirectly affecting treatment reliability and patient outcomes.


This is why purchasing in pharma is not a “cost center.” It’s a risk-management function with real-world consequences.

Here’s the shift that changes your day-to-day reality:

What this means for you in practice:


- Cost savings through simplification: You reduce complexity in purchasing, qualification, and ongoing supplier management. Fewer suppliers means fewer audits, fewer contracts, fewer coordination loops and lower total cost of ownership, not just piece price.Simplified supplier base: No multi-sourcing puzzle where each component has to match perfectly. One source, one SKU strategy, one set of technical interfaces, less administrative and operational load.
- Improved vendor relationship and accountability: When something happens, you don’t mediate between suppliers. You have a single accountable partner who owns the system performance, documentation, and supply reliability. That reduces internal escalation and strengthens your position externally.
- Reliable supply and streamlined compliance: A fully integrated syringe system supports consistency, quality control, and documentation alignment, making compliance easier to maintain and easier to defend.


The real benefit is psychological as much as operational: you remove categories of uncertainty. You spend less time coordinating and more time steering, optimizing contracts, forecasting intelligently, and building true resilience.


#### Because your job isn’t to “buy parts.”


Your job is to ensure the system works - on time, on budget, in compliance, without surprises.


And that becomes significantly easier when the syringe system comes from one accountable source.
